title: Drishyam 3 Reviews: Critics Call the Finale Gripping, Hail Ajay Devgn–Jaideep Ahlawat Face-Off
excerpt: Critics largely praise the final chapter of the Drishyam franchise, with the Ajay Devgn–Jaideep Ahlawat showdown and the climax earning the strongest notices, even as some reviewers flag a slow first half and convenient plotting.
body:
• The consensus: 18 published critic reviews average 3.5/5 — ranging from 2.5 (Rediff) to 4.5 (Taran Adarsh, Glamsham), with most mainstream critics landing at 3 to 3.5 stars.
  • What's praised: the Ajay Devgn–Jaideep Ahlawat face-off, the courtroom sequences, a climax critics say delivers, and strong turns from Tabu and Prakash Raj.
  • What's criticized: a slow first half, convenient plotting that asks viewers to take too much at face value, and an ear-shattering background score.
  • What this means for you: the film is in cinemas now (released October 2, runtime 2 hours 30 minutes). If you liked the first two films, critics say the finale is worth a theatre watch for the climax — but expect a slow build before the payoff.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BSZZwBaNQAA

A broadly positive verdict

The reviews for Drishyam: The Conclusion are in, and the final chapter of the franchise has landed well with critics. Across 18 published reviews tracked by The Videshi, the film averages 3.5 stars out of 5 — a solid, if not ecstatic, consensus.

https://x.com/ajaydevgn/status/2105689164490666309

The most enthusiastic notices come from trade-leaning reviewers. Taran Adarsh, writing for Bollywood Hungama, gave the film 4.5 stars, calling it "OUTSTANDING" and "without doubt, the BEST FILM in the Drishyam franchise and also among the BEST FILMS of 2026," declaring it a "SURE-SHOT BLOCKBUSTER." Glamsham matched the 4.5 rating.

MensXP, Filmibeat, TellyChakkar and The Week India each gave 4 stars. The mainstream press was more measured: The Times of India, CinemaExpress, IndiaForums, IWMBuzz, ABP News and Moneycontrol all landed at 3.5, while NDTV's Saibal Chatterjee, The Indian Express's Shubhra Gupta, Hindustan Times and India Today gave 3 stars. Rediff's Sukanya Verma was the outlier at 2.5.

What critics loved: the face-off, the courtroom, the climax

One point of near-universal agreement: the confrontation between Ajay Devgn's Vijay Salgaonkar and Jaideep Ahlawat's crime-branch officer Rajveer Singh Tomar is the film's high point.

"The biggest high point is the Ajay Devgn – Jaideep Ahlawat face-off in the first half. Simply MARVELLOUS. Deserves a standing ovation!"

— Taran Adarsh, Bollywood Hungama

NDTV's Saibal Chatterjee summed up the casting verdict crisply: "Come for Ajay Devgn, stay for Jaideep Ahlawat. The former delivers the goods. The latter adds weight, the sort that makes an indelible impression."

The courtroom sequences — a franchise first, with Prakash Raj as the prosecutor — drew consistent praise, as did the climax. Bollywood Hungama's review answered its own three questions — "Does it deliver? Does it culminate convincingly? Does it leave you satisfied?" — with "YES, YES, YES," calling the finale "powerful, gripping, and thoroughly fulfilling."

Tabu's return as Meera Deshmukh earned strong notices for a performance of "anger, hurt, revenge, determination," while several critics noted the significance of the original screenplay: unlike the first two films, this finale is not a remake of a Malayalam original but an independently developed Hindi script — a risk the writers largely pull off.

What didn't work: the slow build and convenient plotting

The most common complaint is pacing. Multiple reviewers describe a slow first half — MovieTalkies noted "practically no suspense till the interval point" — with the film taking its time to reach its pressure-cooker finale.

Hindustan Times' Rishabh Suri wrote that for a franchise that "built its reputation on making the impossible seem plausible, this one asks us to take a few too many things at face value." Moneycontrol similarly flagged "convenient solutions and the clues that the police somehow fail to notice," leaving "a few noticeable holes" in the screenplay.

The Indian Express's Shubhra Gupta took aim at the sound design: "If only the film didn't wreathe itself in ear-shattering bgm, I would have liked it even more: why do even the most confidently-told films not trust its telling?" The Times of India added that at two-and-a-half hours, "the film begins to drag towards the end and could have benefited from tighter editing."

The diaspora angle

For the global Indian audience, the Drishyam franchise has long punched above its weight — a middle-class Goan family's cat-and-mouse game with the law that travelled from Kerala's original to Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and even international remakes. That this finale arrives as an original Hindi screenplay rather than another remake is a quiet milestone: Bollywood trusting its own writers to close one of its most beloved franchises. Released on the Gandhi Jayanti holiday, it is positioned as the festive season's big family outing — the rare thriller that plays as well in Toronto and New Jersey multiplexes as in single screens back home.

What's next

The critical consensus points to a film that will live or die on word of mouth around its climax — and early signs are strong. Early estimates put the worldwide opening day at Rs 95.1 crore, and trade analyst Komal Nahta has already called it a "surefire super-hit" that could "surpass the combined business of both the earlier films in the franchise." If the climax delivers for audiences the way it did for critics, Vijay Salgaonkar's final trick may also be his most lucrative.
